conversation.content: Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and understand how life has felt for you since your baby arrived. Today we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question check-in that helps us see how you’re coping emotionally in these first weeks and months postpartum. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want a snapshot of your recent feelings so we can figure out the best support for you. When you’re ready, I’ll ask the first question.

*settles into the chair, hands clasped tightly in my lap, eyes a little red-rimmed*

Okay... thank you. I’ve been looking forward to talking to someone, honestly. I just want to feel like myself again.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slowly, eyes downcast*

Not really... I mean, I can smile when my husband does something silly with the baby, but it's like a quick flash and then it's gone. Nothing feels truly funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs, voice dropping to a near-whisper*

Not much… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower. Now it all feels flat, like I’m going through the motions. I still go, but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*nods, eyes watering*

Yes... all the time. If the baby cries longer than usual, I immediately think it's because I'm not doing something right. When I couldn't breastfeed at first, I kept replaying every decision, wondering what I did wrong. Even little things like forgetting to pack a diaper, I tell myself I'm a terrible mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*wrings hands in lap*

All the time. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly picture her choking, or I’ll wake up sure the blanket has moved over her face. There’s no real reason—she’s healthy, the monitor’s on—but the thoughts just race. I check her breathing over and over, even when I know it’s fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*nods quickly, voice trembling*

Yes... it hits out of nowhere. Last night I was rocking the baby in the dark and my heart started pounding so hard I thought I might pass out. Nothing happened—no noise, no fever, nothing—but for a few minutes I was sure something awful was about to happen.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods, shoulders sagging*

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is due, plus the laundry and texts I haven’t answered. I keep lists, but they just get longer. Some mornings I lie there thinking, “I can’t climb this mountain again today,” even though nothing’s huge on its own—it’s just all of it together.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*exhales shakily*

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off. I replay every little thing I did with her—did I burp her long enough, was the swaddle too tight—then I start worrying about tomorrow. By the time I drift off, she’s usually ready to wake up again.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice cracks, eyes welling up*

Pretty much every day. I wake up with this heaviness, like there’s a weight on my chest. I see the sun out and hear her coo, and I still feel… gray. I keep thinking, “I should be happy—she’s here, she’s safe,” but the sadness just sits there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*presses a tissue to eyes*

Twice this week. Yesterday my husband asked what’s wrong and I couldn’t even explain—it just spilled out. And the day before, she wouldn’t nap, and I sat on the nursery floor crying with her in my arms, feeling like I’m failing at the one thing she needs.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*looks down, voice barely audible*

A couple of times… nothing planned, just—when I’m rocking her at 3 a.m. and everything feels hopeless—this quick flash of “what if I just disappeared?” It scares me; I don’t want to leave her, but the thought sneaks in for a second before I push it away.

You've shared that since your baby arrived laughter feels distant and life has turned gray; activities you once enjoyed now feel flat and the days often seem an overwhelming mountain of feeding lists and self-doubt. Despite loving your daughter you wake each morning with a heavy chest carry constant worry about her safety and have moments when despair gives way to tears or frightening thoughts of disappearing.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only fleeting smiles, no genuine laughter or sustained enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely not so much now".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure—activities once enjoyed now feel 'flat' and lack any 'spark,' aligning with 'Hardly at all.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive self-blame across multiple daily situations, consistent with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, excessive worry about the baby choking or suffocating, checking repeatedly despite reassurance, indicating anxiety "very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic while calmly caring for baby, classic nocturnal panic attack</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to keep up with daily tasks, and waking with dread—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts and persistent insomnia tied to unhappiness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "pretty much every day" and persistent emotional heaviness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying twice in the past week and feeling unable to control or explain the tears, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 27/30 places you well above the high-risk cut-off of 13; scores on items 3-8 are maximal indicating persistent <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>loss of pleasure</sym>, <sym>self-blame</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic</sym> and <sym>feeling overwhelmed</sym> that align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Item 10 ≥1 mandates immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Develop a written safety plan and keep 24/7 crisis numbers handy
3. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or sertraline compatible with breastfeeding
4. Schedule brief daily walks and accept help with night feeds to improve sleep
5. Involve your partner or trusted adult in monitoring warning signs
6. Book follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (partner present)  
Date: [today’s date]  
Screener: [name, credentials]  

I. Presenting symptoms endorsed (≥ 2-week duration inferred)  
- Persistent low mood, “heaviness,” daily crying spells  
- Marked anhedonia (minimal enjoyment of baby, partner, or prior interests)  
- Excessive, inappropriate guilt/self-blame regarding infant care  
- Intrusive, catastrophic worries (“terrible things will happen”)  
- Recurrent panic-like episodes (physiologic arousal, sense of doom)  
- Sleep-onset insomnia secondary to rumination  
- Feeling overwhelmed, unable to “climb the mountain” of routine tasks  

II. Observations  
- Flat affect, tearfulness, psychomotor slowing  
- Frequent safety-relevant intrusive thought (“what if I disappeared?”)  
- No current suicidal plan or intent; thoughts transient but distressing  

III. Screening significance  
- Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (if scored) likely ≥ 12 (high)  
- Meets DSM-5-TR screening criteria for Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset and comorbid anxiety features  
- Self-harm cognitions present → elevated risk category  

IV. Risk factors identified  
- First-time mother, feeding difficulties, self-criticism  
- Limited perceived social support (husband unaware of distress depth)  
- Prior sleep deprivation amplifying mood instability  

V. Safety / next steps (screening level)  
- Immediate safety plan reviewed; patient denies intent/act  
- Recommend expedited referral to perinatal psychiatry/therapy for comprehensive evaluation and possible medication discussion  
- Provide crisis resources (24/7 hotline, ED if worsening)  
- Partner instructed on warning signs (increased hopelessness, withdrawal, any self-harm plan)  

Overall impression: High likelihood of moderate–severe perinatal depression with comorbid anxiety; safety risk present though not imminent; prompt specialty follow-up indicated.
